claude.via: Claude Code subagent (Agent tool), not the API

claude.reason: A ruling by Rav Yehuda and a debate about it; the incident behind it is only named, nothing of it told.
An incident alluded to ('there was an incident like this') with its outcome (they required halitza); sketched only by reference to the case under discussion.
Gemara terminology clarification and Rabbi Hiyya's teachings; no event.
Legal discussion of the David and Bathsheba incident, only alluded to; no narration, and biblical in any case.
Reports of what sages said and practiced regarding orla abroad, with nothing following; no story.
Orphans come before Rava, he rules, the Sages challenge and he answers; coming before him is the only event, the rest is legal dialogue.
An eyewitness incident (a yevama came to perform halitza before Rabbi Tarfon) followed by his instruction; one real event, mainly speech, cited as a proof.
A certain man picking dates, a woman asks, a betrothal exchange and Rav Zevid's ruling; real events but mainly dialogue.
A halakhic question and answer between Rava bar Rav Hanan and Abaye; no event.
Legal statements and a baraita describing a hypothetical case; nothing that happened.
Beit Hillel's ruling on Queen Helene is cited as a terminological proof; the incident itself is not told in the text.
An eyewitness account: a woman came before Ameimar seeking a tenth of the estate, her brothers responded, Ameimar was silent; mainly speech with a sibling dispute, cited as evidence of his view.
A certain man gave a conditional bill of divorce, the thirty days passed and he claimed he tried to marry her; some events, mainly speech, outcome left to discussion.
Two eyewitness reports of being given food that was brought to a master, otherwise endangered; real events with little change, cited as evidence for a rule.
Someone came before Rav Yosef, he ruled, and Abaye challenged; coming before him is the only event, the rest is ordinary legal dialogue.
A Mehoza woman married into Neharde'a comes before Rav Nahman, who recognizes her accent and rules, then reverses when told of her marriage; mainly speech but with events and a change.
Exegetical derivation of Moses' birth and death dates from verses; not a narrative, and biblical.
A woman seized a silver cup toward her ketubah, demanded sustenance and came before Rava, who ruled for her; an incident plus ruling with a small change.
A scribe comes before Rabbi Abbahu confessing improper parchment preparation and the scroll is disqualified; prior events are told only within the dialogue, but there is a resulting change.
A legal dilemma, a search for a source and a sent ruling; study and teaching are speech, not events.
Rav Hanina states a halakha and Rabbi Yannai rebukes him; a sharp retort is ordinary Talmudic discourse, not conflict for a story.
Medical advice Abaye reports from his foster mother; general teaching, no event.
Rabbi Hiyya taught a halakha in two attributions and was or was not praised; teaching and reception are speech, used to infer the halakha.

Rabbi Elazar reports Rav's ruling to Shmuel and is mocked; later Rabbi Zeira travels to the Land of Israel, finds it taught there and remarks on it; mainly speech, with travel and an arc of vindication.
Rav Nahman's visit to Sura only frames a halakhic question-and-answer exchange; no event beyond speech.

A man whose levirate obligation falls abroad comes before R. Hanina and is answered; coming before the rabbi is the only narrated event besides the background condition, so per R-C0's limit there is no story.
Conflicting attributions of rulings and legal dialectic; no event is narrated.
Transmission of a teaching and a correction of its context; teaching and speech only, no event or conflict beyond ordinary scholarly exchange.
Ravina finds Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak pondering a halakhic dilemma that stays unresolved; a scene framing a legal question with no event that leads anywhere.
A baraita on a general custom and legal rules about wedding days; no particular incident is narrated.

One real event (R. Hiyya bar Ami's slave immersed a gentile woman) followed by Rav Yosef's ruling that changes her and her daughter's status; one event plus ruling with an implied change. Segment 5 is separate name-calling cases with rulings only.
A mis-transmitted ruling is sent and corrected by recalling how a teaching was given; all speech and transmission of teaching, no event beyond speaking.

Rabbis about to act on a baraita are stopped by an old woman recounting her own incident before Rav Nahman; mainly dialogue but events are mentioned and an implied change results. Segment 3 is Gemara discussion.
R. Abba teaches, Rav Safra objects, and the answer is traced up a chain of questions; standard scholarly dialogue with no event.
The Sages sought to permit the Gibeonites and Rabbi answered with an argument; ordinary halakhic debate, speech only, no narrated event or change.
People called two men by derogatory names and rabbis answered with a legal argument; speech and ruling only, with no other narrated action or change.

The death of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: the fast and prayers, the maidservant throwing the jug to silence the prayers, his death, bar Kappara's announcement, and his last prayer answered by a heavenly voice; multiple actions with causality and change.
A mishna cited as an objection, stating hypothetical legal rules; no event.
Rav Hisda's habitual response when such cases came before him, followed by Gemara discussion; a custom that leads nowhere, not a particular incident.

A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, Hasa died without instructions, they came before Rav Nahman who ruled for the depositor; an incident with more than one narrated action followed by a ruling, the R-C0 shape.
An incident is only named as having come before R. Yitzhak in Antioch; nothing of it is told, only his ruling.
Bar Haddaya consults R. Ahai and then R. Ami and R. Asi, who give differing rulings; consulting rabbis is the only event, the rest is speech.
Abaye's boast and a Sage's challenge lead into a halakhic exchange; ordinary scholarly dialogue with no event.
R. Tarfon's eyewitness account of ascending the platform and hearing the High Priest conceal the Name has real actions but little causality or change, framed by a general account of the practice.
R. Elazar asks an elder a question about a past ruling; the incident is only named, and the passage is speech.
R. Zeira avoided his teacher Rav Yehuda because he wished to emigrate against his teacher's view; a real action with conflict, but nothing follows within the passage.
Rava coerced the wealthy Rav Natan bar Ami and collected four hundred dinars for charity, cited as a precedent; an action with a result, but very brief and serving as evidence for a ruling.
Gemara analysis of a mishna's wording; no event.
R. Ami and R. Asi intended to rule and R. Yaakov bar Idi rebuked them; an intended ruling and a rebuke are ordinary rabbinic dialogue, not a story.
A man states his origin, R. Yitzhak Nappaha stands and identifies the place, then legal-geographic discussion; speech only, no event or change.
Within a dialogue, an incident is sketched: a debtor hid his money behind a gentile and the Sages in turn forced him to sell land. Two actions with a consequence, but only alluded to inside speech.
A bare report of how Ravina collected a dowry, cited as legal proof; no one responds and nothing follows.
A rabbi states a ruling and another rebukes it with a verse; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no event.
Rav Ami's permission, the Sages' objection and his answer are mostly speech; there is some conflict and implied change, so borderline rather than not.
A baraita reporting a dispute and that Rabbi ruled one way, then a statement of halakha; no narrated event.
A general legal prescription for a hypothetical case, not an event that happened.
A scribe who wrote a faulty Torah scroll that was sold comes before Rabbi Ami and loses his wage; one real prior event plus a ruling with a consequence, but mainly dialogue.
Coming before Rabbi Ami and his ruling is the only event; no other narrated action or change.
An exchange of letters on a halakhic point with a sharp retort; quasi-speech and ordinary scholarly debate, no event.
A general ruling about kidnapped women and the Rabbis' objections; hypothetical legal discussion, no incident.
Rabba reports finding scholars discussing a dispute and his reply; purely legal discussion, no event.
Embedded in the letter is an incident: a man suffering for love of a woman sought to leave the Land, heard this teaching, and stayed suffering until his death; actions, causality and change.
Legal statement and analysis about minor converts; no narrative.
The orphan daughters come before Shmuel and he rules; coming before him is the only event (Jeff's ruling on Ketubot 50b:4).
The passage is only the opening words of a will's citation; nothing is narrated within it.
A statement of a general custom of David's soldiers with a scriptural derivation; no one-time event.
A chain of hypothetical legal dilemmas; nothing happened.
Legal analysis of a hypothetical scenario of a general coming to town; no actual event.
A constructed legal case about successive witnesses, stated to explain a dispute; hypothetical, not an event.
A man's will, then the dowry price falls, then a ruling on the surplus; one real event followed by a ruling with a consequence, but minimal.
Legal inference about sustenance obligations in hypothetical cases.
Institutional history: the priests' court raised the widow's ketubah, men stopped marrying widows, the court reversed; events with causality and change, but collective and schematic.
A man testifies before Reish Lakish about someone reading first in the synagogue, and Rabbi Elazar objects; mainly speech, part of a larger incident continued after the passage.
A woman comes before Ameimar and her brothers speak while he stays silent, cited as evidence of his view; coming before him is the only event.
A report of Mar Zutra's practice and an objection, then a ruling; no continuation (Jeff's ruling on Yevamot 106b).
A son questions his father's ruling and is told to be silent; pure speech, an ordinary scholarly challenge and rebuke with no event.
The Gemara names the Mishnah's incident and derives halakhot from it; the incident is only named here and the passage is legal commentary.
A legal inference and an objection citing a hypothetical mishnaic case; nothing happened.
A Mishnaic ruling and an exposition delivered before the Sages; teaching only, no event.
Rabbi falls ill and is moved to Tzippori, real events, but they are cited within a discussion resolving a contradiction, a fragment of the larger story of his death.
Students ask Rabbi Eliezer a halakhic question and he answers; speech only, followed by commentary.
A Mishnaic legal case framed hypothetically ('one who marries...') with a dispute among Sages; not an event that happened.
Ravina holds an orphan's wine, is taking his own to sell, asks Rav Ashi and is told to go; one action plus a ruling with only an implied change.
Rabbi falls ill, Rabbi Hiyya visits and finds him weeping (emotion counts), questions him and Rabbi explains; a narrated deathbed incident.
The Sages award Nakdimon's daughter a large perfume allowance and she responds with a blessing they answer; an actual incident, but mostly a ruling and speech.
Ben Azzai is challenged for not marrying and defends himself; speech only but with personal conflict. Segments 2-3 are teachings.
A goat drank blacksmith's water and was found with no spleen when slaughtered; real events with a change, but a bare anecdote cited as evidence for a remedy.
The Sidon tanner incident: one event (death leaving a tanner levir) followed by the Sages' ruling with an implied change.
Ravina, holding an orphan's wine and taking his own to sell, consults Rav Ashi and is told to go; an action plus a ruling with an implied change.
Descriptions of former wedding customs in Judea and Galilee; customs with no event following.
A document is brought before Rava and Rav Pappa testifies it was paid; one event and then all dialogue and a ruling.
Rava's retraction supported by a baraita describing a hypothetical legal procedure; no narrated event.
A man asks Rabbi Hanina about a levirate case and is answered; coming before the rabbi is the only event, with the ruling as speech.
Rav Hisda tells Rabba to research a baraita and he does; study and teaching only, no real event.
A hypothetical legal case and a dispute with a ruling; nothing happened.
The freed sons of Yudan are permitted to marry each other's wives and Rava challenges the ruling; one event and a ruling, mostly speech.
A man testifies before Rabbi Ami about another's reading order and Rabbi Ami elevates him to priesthood; mainly dialogue but the ruling produces a change.
Rabba found scholars discussing and offered his view; ordinary scholarly debate, no event.
Legal explanation of a mishnaic clause; no event.
A brief legal inference about the Israelites sacrificing the omer before eating; not a story, and biblical in any case.
A report of Rav Ashi's practice of reciting the wedding blessings, cited as halakhic precedent; nothing follows or changes.
An incident is only named (Rabbi gave one-twelfth) as evidence in a legal argument; nothing of it is narrated.
A habitual practice of what Rava would say to such fathers; speech only, no particular event or change.
Legal discussion of a baraita and the opinions of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel; no narrated event.
Transmission dispute about Rava's ruling with a sarcastic retort; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, speech only.
A description of rabbis' seating arrangement followed only by a teaching and discussion, as Jeff ruled on Yevamot 17a.
A real event (holding his wife's hand through the siege of Jerusalem) followed by the Sages' rejection of his testimony, implying she is forbidden to him; mainly speech, and a Mishnah story (R-C1).
Pishon's wife's refusal is one act cited in debate without change or causality, as Jeff ruled on Yevamot 107b.
Mainly the sending of a halakhic question and its answer, but a real event intervenes: Rav Huna died before it arrived and his son answered instead.
A document brought before Rabbi Abbahu who considered validating it and was corrected; coming before a rabbi and a ruling/objection is the only event.
A yevama falls to a man and his brother seeks to disqualify her; real situation with conflict, but the passage is mostly negotiation dialogue with no resolution narrated.
One action (Rabbi Zeira avoiding Rav Yehuda) followed by the explanation for it; per Jeff on Ketubot 110b, 'just one action and then explanation'.
Reports of habitual practices of standing before elders, cited as halakhic evidence; nothing follows.
Rav Nahman arrives in Sura and is asked a halakhic question which he answers; only speech and ordinary discussion.
A hypothetical legal case in exegesis of a verse; nothing happened.
Orphans come before Rava, who rules, and the Sages challenge the ruling; coming before the rabbi is the only event, with no other narrated action or change.
The Gemara's commentary questioning the preceding story of the man who fell; not part of the story itself.
A man comes before Rabban Gamliel claiming an unobstructed orifice and receives a parable in reply; an underlying event but mainly speech, like Jeff's Ketubot 10a borderline.
Incidents only named as coming before Rabbi and Rabbi Yishmael with their rulings, then scholarly discussion; no other narrated action.
A man comes before Rabban Gamliel claiming an unobstructed orifice and receives a parable in reply; an underlying event but mainly speech, like Jeff's Ketubot 10a borderline.
Mishnah ruling and extended legal analysis; the Rebecca verse is used only as exegesis; no narrated event.
A report of Rav's practice of sustaining orphan girls, followed by a dilemma about its meaning; nothing follows.
An incident is only named in support of a ruling; not enough is narrated.
A girl goes to draw water and is raped, then a ruling on her eligibility; events with weak causality and little change, as Jeff ruled on Ketubot 14b; Mishnah story (R-C1).
Rav Yehuda's habitual difficulty signing and Ulla's advice citing others' practice; speech and reported practice with no change.
A halakhic dilemma raised by Reish Lakish and left unresolved; no event is narrated.
The Tzaidan incident is only named here and the Gemara asks why it is cited; per Jeff on Gittin 46a, an incident only named is not a story.
A bill of divorce is sent as a question to Rabba, who rules. Sending a question is a quasi-speech act, and nothing else happens besides the ruling.
Two brief reports, Rav Kahana taking a cloth and Mar bar Rav Ashi buying one, are cited as evidence for a legal point. Nothing follows from either act and no change results.
A hypothetical case the Gemara constructs ('with what case are we dealing'), not an event that happened.
A report of what Rav Kahana did (delayed selling an orphan's beer) with his rationale; a single act with no consequence or change narrated.
A dispute between Rav and Shmuel told as a scholarly exchange; speech only, with no event and no conflict beyond ordinary debate.
Analysis of why Abaye and Rava chose different sources; pure legal discussion.

A man claims to come from Shot Mishot and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha stands up and declares the place's status, implicitly confirming the man's lineage. It is mainly speech followed by legal discussion, with a small event and an implied change.
A description of Rav Ashi's practice with the wedding blessings at Rav Kahana's; a custom that leads nowhere.
A rumor circulates that a woman was betrothed with a mat of dates, and the case is sent to Abaye, who rules that the rumor is suppressed. One event followed by a ruling that changes her status.
Rava's coercing Rav Natan bar Ami to give charity is cited in one line as precedent for a ruling. Nothing further is narrated.
Homiletic teachings about fingers and ears; no event is narrated.

The Gemara quotes the Mishnah's incident of a bill of divorce with Samaritan witnesses brought before Rabban Gamliel, who validated it. Jeff ruled that the Talmud's quotation of a Mishnah story at Gittin 10b can be included.

A man deposits pearls with Rabbi Meyasha, who dies without instructions, and the parties come before Rabbi Ami, who rules. Several narrated events and a resolution make this an incident followed by a ruling.
Rav Hisda's statement about his own early marriage is a self-report and boast; no narrated incident.
Enactments, an instruction from Rav and Abaye's mother's teachings; speech and law only, no event.
Tannaitic dispute and Amoraic analysis on teruma sustenance; no narrative.
Rabbi Natan asks Sumakhos a legal question and receives a reasoned answer; speech only, with no conflict.
Rav Safra's and Rava's habitual Shabbat preparations are cited as illustrations; customs with no event following.
Rav Kahana taking a cloth at a redemption and declaring it worth five sela is a single act cited as precedent, with no consequence narrated.
Two brief first-person anecdotes: a dish is brought to the master and he shares it, which spared the speaker danger. These are real events but are thin, with the change only implied.
The Upper Galilee men's daily provision of meat is a habitual practice that leads to no change; the rest is Gemara discussion of the amount.

A man betroths a woman with a bundle of rags and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya examines its value to decide the betrothal. It is an incident and a rabbinic response, with the outcome given only conditionally, followed by discussion.
Legal analysis of the practical difference between two opinions; no event.
A situation (people sinning with a maidservant) is described, then Abaye states what he would have done and Ravina comments; nothing further happens and nothing changes.
Abaye's retort to Ravin's report is ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, pure speech with no event.
A rumor and a precedent cited only by its ruling; no narrated action or change beyond the legal decision.
The Sages apportion wine to Nakdimon's daughter-in-law, she blesses them, and they pointedly withhold their amen: several actions with a response and implied conflict.
Pure legal analysis of konamot and liens; no event.
A man comes before Rav Nahman with a claim and Rav Nahman orders him flogged: mainly speech, but an action and consequence follow; segment 3 is Gemara discussion.
A ruling issued by Rabbi Yohanan and discussion of its terminology; no narrated event.
Judges ruled and collected from movable property, and Rav Nahman threatened them to reverse it: events with conflict but weak causality and no narrated outcome.
Legal reasoning, plus brief cases where people called someone a name and a rabbi ruled; the name-calling is speech and the ruling is the only response, with no further action or change.
Legal debate between Rav Yosef, Abaye and Rava; no event.
Rabbi Simlai's remark to his host is a single statement used as a proof, with no conflict and no event.

Rav Malkiyyu married off a deaf-mute and wrote a marriage contract for the woman, which Rava praised: a real act with a change (a marriage), but reported as a precedent and followed by legal reasoning.
Dicta of Rabbi Elazar, plus a remark he made on seeing a field; seeing and speaking leads nowhere and nothing changes.
The passage holds only the end of the story (Rabbi Yonatan forced the sons to feed their father) followed by Gemara analysis; it is part of a story, not all of it.
An incident is only named by its ruling (Rabbi gave one-twelfth), then discussed; nothing of it is narrated.

Rav Hanan visits Rav Kahana, sees an animal before him, and challenges him; Rav Kahana answers. This is mainly dialogue, but real events (a visit, a situation seen) occur alongside the habits of Abaye and Rav Sheshet.
Legal analogies and objections about consecration; no event.
A teaching exchange between Rav Yehezkel and his son, then Shmuel's rebuke: all dialogue and ordinary scholarly correction, with no event.
Rabba bar bar Hana brings a bill of divorce before Rabbi Elazar, who rules; coming before the rabbi and the ruling are the only events, and nothing changes.
Legal discussion of a groom's claim; no event.
A chain of halakhic dilemmas; no event.
Scholarly argument over Rav Sheshet's ruling; ordinary dialogue with no event.
Levi expounds a ruling in Rabbi's name and is not praised, then in the majority's name and is praised: the main actions are teaching, but there is a response and a change.
The incident in the wagons of Tzippori is only alluded to as the setting of a ruling, then explained legally; not enough of it is told.
The Gemara's explanation of what Rabbi Akiva was thinking about the etrog is commentary on a report, not a story.
A woman obligated to an oath comes before Rav Beivai's court; after that it is all dialogue and a ruling, followed by Rav Pappi's rebuke. Mainly speech with a real incident behind it.
A legal discussion of minors' conversion with an objection and a resolution; nothing is narrated.
A scholarly exchange about a hypothetical deer on a Festival. It is speech only, with no conflict and no event.

This continues Reish Lakish's condolence visit: he tells his disseminator to speak and the man recites blessings. It is part of a story but almost entirely speech, and segment 4 is Abaye's comment rather than story.
A question sent by letter and answered in Rabbi's presence. This is quasi-speech and ordinary scholarly exchange with no conflict or change.
A bare report of how Ravina collected the dowry, cited as proof for a halakhic question. Nothing follows from it.
A halakhic objection from a mishna; no narrative.
An incident is only sketched: Rafram pressures Rav Ashi, who then makes the creditor pay full value. There is a real action and a resulting change, but very little of the incident is told.
Two rabbis struggle with a problem for 22 years until Rav Yosef becomes head of the academy and resolves it. There is an event and a change, but the passage is mainly about teaching.

Rav Huna and Rav Nahman visit the sick Rabba bar Avuh and question him. The visit and departure are real events, but the passage is mostly dialogue without real conflict, and segment 4 is Gemara commentary.

A wife's marriage contract is lost and the couple come before Rav Yosef, who rules. The loss is a real event beyond coming to court, but the passage gives only the start of the incident and then a ruling.

A man sets a deadline for a conditional divorce, fails to marry by it, and then claims he meant a different month, followed by legal analysis. It is mostly speech with some conflict and an implied event.
A legal explanation of a mishna; no narrative.
Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef finds Rabbi Abbahu at Usha and learns the halakha forty times. Something happens, but the passage is mainly about teaching, which the editor rules borderline.
One act (a betrothal with vegetables in the marketplace) followed by Ravina's ruling and legal discussion, with no further action or change.
A mishna listing a wife's duties and legal opinions; nothing is narrated.
Rabbi Yohanan objects to Rabbi Elazar's teaching, is grieved, and Rabbi Elazar finds a remedy in response. It is mainly dialogue, but it has conflict, an emotional reaction and a change.
A fragment of Rabbi's last illness: he falls ill and is moved to Tzippori, with a burial place ready in Beit She'arim. The events and change are embedded in the Gemara's harmonizing discussion.
Rabbi Yosei travels to Netzivin, meets an elder, and questions him about Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's practice. There are real events, but it is mainly dialogue and is told as halakhic evidence.
A question put to Rabbi Yohanan and his answer, then a ruling. It is speech only, with no conflict.
A halakhic dilemma; no narrative.
One act (Rav Kahana holds an orphan's beer until the Festival) and his explanation for it. No outcome or change is narrated.

Rav Hamnuna teaches, the whole hall clamors against him, and Rav Yosef defends him, after which Hamnuna praises Rav Yosef. It is speech with public conflict that is more than routine debate, and it is resolved.
One act (Rav Haviva recites a blessing at a circumcision) followed by a ruling against him. No change follows.
Derivation of verses for the grooms' benediction. Shmuel's instruction to Rav Hana is only cited as a teaching.
Rav Nahman's arrival in Sura is only the frame for a halakhic question-and-answer; ordinary scholarly dialogue with no event or change beyond speech.

A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, who died without instructions, and the claimant came before Rabbi Abba who ruled; narrated incident with more than one action followed by a ruling, like R-C0's cow case.
Legal discussion of remarriage rules; the strangling incident is only named in a clause as evidence, with nothing of it told.
A general dictum about bringing children to school and its reconciliation; no narrated event.
Legal objection and answer about fines and converts; no event happened.
Legal discussion of wedding benedictions; Boaz is cited only as a scriptural proof, not narrated.
A baraita on yields and a Sadducee's remark praising the land; speech only, without conflict or event.
Rav objects to Shmuel's father, who is silent, and Rav applies a verse to him; ordinary scholarly challenge, not conflict in R-C2's sense, and no event.
Abaye's boast and a Sage's exegetical challenge with his answer; standard rabbinic dialogue with no event.

A man testifies before R. Yehoshua ben Levi about another's reading second in synagogue, and the rabbi elevates that man to Levite status; mostly dialogue and a ruling, but a real event and a resulting change in status.
Rav Huna finds the Sages discussing and disputes their view; finding them is a frame for teaching and debate, no real event.
Legal discussion of defects in the sale of slaves; no narrative.

Rabba bar Rav Huna teaches publicly, is challenged by Rav Hisda, then appoints an interpreter and retracts publicly; mainly teaching and speech but with an action and a change (Gittin 43a ruled low confidence at most).
Rabbi Zeira's travel only frames hearing a teaching from Rabbi Asi; teaching is speech and nothing happens.
Rabbi Elazar considers a ruling and a student advises against it; speech and ordinary scholarly caution with no narrated event or outcome.
Rav Kahana brings a bill of divorce and asks Rav whether he must make the declaration; coming before the rabbi with a question and a ruling, with no change resulting.
A man's claim of impurity brought before Rabbi Ami, his ruling, and Rabbi Asi's challenge; coming before the rabbi is the only event, and the rest is legal dialogue.
Legal discussion of the reasons for a mishnaic ruling; no event.
A woman comes before Ameimar, her brothers speak and he is silent, cited as evidence of his view; coming before the rabbi is the only event, with no change narrated.
Explanation of a historical government decree as the background of a custom, with legal reasoning; no narrated incident about particular people.
A difficulty unresolved for twenty-two years until Rav Yosef became head of the academy and resolved it; mainly about teaching, but becoming head is a real event and the resolution is a change.
Rav Yehuda's teaching exchanges with his son about his wife and the Gemara's reconciliation; speech only, no event.
Legal discussion of wedding celebration days; no narrative.
Rav Yosef mixing seeds is one action followed by a legal discussion and a retraction in argument; Jeff ruled Kiddushin 39a 'one action followed by a legal discussion', not a story.
Legal discussion of Shmuel's rulings on vows; no event.
A man whose betrothed died comes before the rabbis and is ruled on; coming before them is the only narrated event, and the rest is ordinary halakhic objection (R-C0's limit).
A Mishnah stating a hypothetical law and a dispute; nothing happened.
An incident is only named as having come before Rabbi Yitzhak; nothing of it is told, only his ruling.
Bare reports of how many blessings two sages recited at weddings, cited as evidence of practice; nothing follows.
A custom is cited and illustrated by a report of someone smearing oil at a wedding, plus an ordinary scholarly retort; no event leads anywhere.
An incident is only alluded to ('I was involved in an incident') with the sages' ruling; nothing of it is narrated.
The sages added cups, people became drunk, and the ordinance was reverted: events with a change, though told as institutional history with minimal narrative.
Cases came before Rabbi and Rabbi Yishmael and they ruled; coming before them is the only event, followed by scholarly discussion.
Transmission of a teaching and a disagreement about its context; speech only, ordinary scholarly exchange.
Ameimar's permission, Rav Ashi's challenge and the explanation are rulings and debate with no narrated event.
Bare reports of how many blessings two sages recited at weddings, cited as evidence of practice; nothing follows.
A report of Rav Zevid's ruling or practice, cited as evidence; no response or consequence.
Halakhic objection and resolution about hypothetical cases; nothing happened.
Ravina holds an orphan's wine, is taking his own to sell, and asks Rav Ashi, who tells him to go; real events but mainly a question and ruling, with the change at best implied.
A halakhic exchange between Rav Pappi and Rav Pappa; ordinary scholarly debate, no event.
Two terse cases: a man's bequest, a change in prices, and a ruling on who gets the difference; real events with a change, but little more than a case and ruling.
A woman rebelled, Mar Zutra compelled her to stay, and Rabbi Hanina of Sura was born of the couple: a narrated incident with action and consequence (the Gemara's closing remark is commentary).
A man whose betrothed died comes before the rabbis and is ruled on; coming before them is the only narrated event, and the rest is ordinary halakhic objection (R-C0's limit).
The sages reclining in Lod debate study versus action and reach a collective decision; mainly speech, with a dispute and a resolution.
Levi intended to rule by a baraita and Rav corrected him with a tradition; speech and ruling only.
A found bill of divorce and Rabba's ruling on it: one event followed by a ruling and discussion of the details, with no resulting change narrated.
Shapur's daughter's mother ate etrogim and the daughter was so fragrant she was placed before her father among the spices: events with causality, but told in a single line as illustration.
A hypothetical legal case from a baraita ('if one's bread was baked... and the father died'); not an event that happened.
A man comes before Rabbi Hanina with a question and receives a sharp ruling; coming before the rabbi is the only event (R-C0's limit).
A question put to Rabbi Yehoshua, his evasive answer and testimony about families; speech in ordinary halakhic exchange with no narrated event.
Mainly an exchange between the Rabbis and R. Abba bar Zavda, but a real event (his becoming impotent from Rav Huna's discourse) explains his refusal; mostly speech with something happening.
Only a couple coming before Rav Yosef and beginning their claims; coming before a rabbi is the only event in the passage.
Shmuel's instruction to Rav Hana to gather ten men is cited as halakhic precedent; speech and teaching only, no narrated event or change.
The incident in Tzippori is only named as a location for a halakhic point; nothing of it is told.
Baraita halakha and Gemara analysis about sleeping arrangements; no narrated event.
R. Yannai rebukes Rav Hanina over a ruling; a rebuke in the study hall is ordinary rabbinic discourse, not a story.
The rabbis travel to Hintzevu, are asked a question, debate, and go before Rav Idi bar Avin; mainly halakhic dialogue, but with real events of arriving and coming before him.
Rabba and Abaye, of Eli's house, engaged in Torah and kindness and lived 40 and 60 years: a habitual practice leading to an outcome, but told as a brief report with weak narration.
A Mehoza woman and her husband come before Rav Nahman, who recognizes her accent and rules, then reverses when told she married into Neharde'a; mostly dialogue but with an event and a change.
The Rabbis urge Rav Sheshet to marry and he deflects; the Gemara adds he had become impotent from Rav Huna's discourse. Mainly speech, with an underlying real event.
One act (betrothal with vegetables in the market) followed by Ravina's ruling and discussion, with no change resulting.
Rav Hisda and Rav Yosef exchange reasoning on a halakhic question; pure scholarly dialogue.
Two deeds come before Rav Yosef and he rules, with the claimant's objections answered; coming before the rabbi is the only event, the rest is legal dialogue.
An incident in which the daughters preceded the sons to Jerusalem, showing the daughters zealous and the sons lazy: actions with an outcome.
The Galileans sending a question to R. Helbo is a quasi-speech act; nothing happens in the passage.
A bare report that Bonyam ben Nunyam sent Rabbi fine fabrics, cited to explain a word; one act with no continuation.
The incident in Tzaidan is only named here and the Gemara asks about the mishna's structure; Jeff ruled this not a story.
A ruling by Rav Zevid, or a bare report that he himself did so; no response or change follows.
A baraita stating a legal case; hypothetical, not an event that happened.
Halakhic dispute between Rav and Shmuel on a deathbed gift; no narrative.
Bar Kappara's exegesis and R. Hiyya's challenge are ordinary scholarly exchange with no event.
A man comes before Rav Nahman with a virginity claim and Rav Nahman orders him flogged; mainly speech acts, but with a consequence for the man.
Rav Pappa's instruction to Pappa the ox herder is cited as a ruling; teaching/ruling without a narrated event or change.
One act (betrothal with silk) followed by a legal dispute between Rabba and Rav Yosef, with no change resulting.
Legal discussion that only alludes to the David and Bathsheba incident as a source; nothing is narrated.
Elijah's advice to Rabbi Natan is pure speech, dietary counsel with no event and no conflict.
Mainly a scholarly exchange, but something happens: Mar Yehuda finds them at the doorway, they fall silent, and they go to Rabba, who rebukes them. Mostly speech with minor events, so borderline.
Pure legal discussion and objection about a hypothetical case; nothing happened.

R. Yohanan's relatives come to him about their stepmother's medical costs, he advises them, and afterwards he regrets having acted as a legal advisor. That is more than one action, and his regret is a change.
Rav Nahman's arrival in Sura only frames a halakhic question and his answer; besides the question nothing happens and nothing changes.
A report of one act (Rav Kahana held the orphan's beer until the festival) plus his rationale. One action and an explanation, with no change or response.
One rabbi praises a ruling and another rebukes the praise. That is ordinary Talmudic dialogue, which Jeff ruled not a story on Ketubot 21b.

The widow who removed her husband from the grave is only alluded to and has to be filled in from the commentaries, so it is borderline per Jeff's ruling on Kiddushin 80b. Segments 2-4 are legal discussion.
A habitual practice (Rav Aha dancing with the bride on his shoulders) followed by a halakhic question and answer. The custom leads to no event or change.
Legal argumentation over hypothetical consecration cases; no event.
A man comes before Rav Nahman with a claim and Rav Nahman orders him flogged. It is mainly speech with a court action implied, matching Jeff's borderline note on Ketubot 10a.

The aftermath of the Mishnah's incident: after the ruling, R. Zekharya housed his wife in his courtyard and arranged their movements around her sons. This is a change resulting from the ruling, but the passage is only part of the story and is told as habitual practice.
